subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Primordial Element Abundances
description: Learn Primordial Element Abundances in one minute.

hook.text: The Big Bang predicted exact ratios: 75% hydrogen, 25% helium, traces of lithium. Measurements match perfectly.

buildup.text: Stars create heavier elements, but the lightest ones trace back to the universe's first three minutes.

discovery.text: Ralph Alpher and George Gamow calculated these abundances in 1948—decades before they could be precisely measured.

twist.text: There's a lithium problem: the Big Bang predicts three times more lithium-7 than we observe. Nobody knows why.

climax.text: Despite the lithium puzzle, the hydrogen-helium ratio is one of the strongest confirmations of Big Bang cosmology.

punchline.text: The recipe from 13.8 billion years ago. We can still read the ingredients.

quiz.question: What is the 'lithium problem' in Big Bang cosmology?
options: The predicted amount of lithium-7 is three times more than what we observe
Lithium should not exist at all according to Big Bang theory
Too much lithium was found in the oldest stars

details.summary: Big Bang nucleosynthesis produced a specific mix of elements: about 75% hydrogen, 25% helium-4, and trace amounts of deuterium, helium-3, and lithium-7. These predicted abundances match observations throughout the universe — one of the Big Bang theory's most precise and compelling confirmations.
details.whyItMatters: Primordial element abundances are a smoking gun for the Big Bang. The precise match between theoretical predictions and observations across the cosmos leaves no reasonable doubt that the universe began in a hot, dense state.
takeaways: The Big Bang produced roughly 75% hydrogen and 25% helium
Trace deuterium, helium-3, and lithium-7 were also created
Predicted ratios precisely match observations everywhere

faq.question: Why is deuterium important for Big Bang evidence?
faq.answer: Deuterium is easily destroyed in stars but not easily created — so all deuterium in the universe is primordial. Its observed abundance directly constrains the density of normal matter in the early universe. This determination independently matches CMB measurements, providing a powerful cross-check.

faq.question: Is there a problem with lithium predictions?
faq.answer: Yes — the 'cosmological lithium problem.' Big Bang nucleosynthesis predicts about 3 times more lithium-7 than observed in old stars. This discrepancy has persisted for decades despite various proposed solutions, including stellar destruction, modified nuclear physics, or new particles.
